Chromatics drives Glorious, Redragon, an: Chromatics drives Glorious, Redragon, and 11 other EVision-family keyboards through the same HID protocol OpenRGB uses. The driver covers Glorious GMMK TKL, Redragon K550 / K552 / K552-2 / K556, Tecware Phantom Elite, Womier K66 / K87, Mars Gaming MKMini, Skillkorp K5, DEXP Blaze, Warrior Kane TC235, and Gamepower Ogre RGB.
How the protocol affects the keyboard: How the protocol affects the keyboard
The keyboard firmware writes colour data: The keyboard firmware writes colour data to its internal storage chip every time the colour changes on the wire. Static colours and slow effects cost nothing. Continuous fast-changing effects (spectrum cycle, audio visualizer, raid animations) write the chip hundreds of times per minute. Over years of continuous use, that wear could shorten the chip lifespan.
OpenRGB has used this same protocol for: OpenRGB has used this same protocol for years and the community has not reported widespread storage-chip failures. The trade-off is real but the practical risk is small for typical use.
If you mostly run static colours or slow: If you mostly run static colours or slow effects, you do not need to do anything. If you plan to run fast-changing effects continuously for hours every day, switch the keyboard off on the Mappings tab when you do not need it. That stops the writes immediately.

QMK keyboards over Raw HID. Covers Novel: QMK keyboards over Raw HID. Covers NovelKeys, KBDFans, Drop, GMMK, Glorious and any other custom keyboard running QMK with Raw HID enabled.
Chromatics didn't detect any QMK keyboar: Chromatics didn't detect any QMK keyboards. Make sure your keyboard is plugged in over USB and that its firmware has Raw HID enabled (the default for any VIA-compatible build). If VIA, Vial, or OpenRGB is running, close it before enabling this provider - they hold the Raw HID interface exclusively. See the console for the full list of detected HID devices.

Chromatics drives QMK devices through tw: Chromatics drives QMK devices through two protocols, chosen automatically based on what the device firmware supports.
Your device acts as a single zone. VIA o: Your device acts as a single zone. VIA only exposes one RGB matrix base colour for the whole device, so it glows one colour at a time even when your Chromatics layers paint per-LED. Most stock firmware lands here, including Keychron vendor builds.
Per-LED control needs the OpenRGB-QMK fi: Per-LED control needs the OpenRGB-QMK firmware module compiled into your QMK build. It is a third-party add-on, not part of stock QMK - you compile it into a custom firmware image and flash that onto your device yourself.
Once flashed, the next Chromatics launch: Once flashed, the next Chromatics launch detects the module during the QMK handshake and switches the device to per-LED direct mode. No Chromatics setting needs to change.
Chromatics does not provide instructions: Chromatics does not provide instructions, support, or pre-built firmware images for the OpenRGB-QMK firmware module. Building and flashing custom firmware is between you, the QMK keymap on the device, and the OpenRGB-QMK project. A bad flash can brick a device - only attempt this if you can recover from one.
If Chromatics detects the QMK Raw HID in: If Chromatics detects the QMK Raw HID interface but the device never responds, the usual firmware-side cause is a RAW_EPSIZE mismatch: the USB descriptor and openrgb.c are compiled with different packet sizes, so the kernel drops every reply at its length check. OpenRGB-QMK upstream convention is 64-byte reports - put OPT_DEFS += -DRAW_EPSIZE=64 in the keymap rules.mk so the 64 reaches every translation unit, not just openrgb.c.
